final_aggregated.Summary: The paper presents CertGate, a selective-prediction gate for multi-site clinical risk models that certifies, with finite-sample confidence 1-delta, that an influence-weighted answered-set error rate — averaged over a population of sites, with the hospital rather than the record as the unit of statistical independence — stays at or below a budget alpha. Each calibration hospital is compressed into one bounded atom tested with a Waudby-Smith-Ramdas betting martingale; the operating threshold is chosen by a fixed-sequence walk over a grid with a two-rung budget ladder (alpha in {0.05, 0.10}). Two assumption modes are shipped: an exchangeable baseline and a BBSE label-shift mode that propagates the estimation uncertainty of four corrected parameters into the guarantee via a Bonferroni box of cluster-robust intervals. A linear head supplies exact additive attributions for both answers and abstentions. Evaluation spans nine synthetic experiment families on a 208-site generator with oracle access (validity, label-shift stress, a verified-falsifiable concept-shift negative control, a site-count frontier, attributions, coverage/composition, a record-as-unit comparator, alternative-bound and stress suites, and power frontiers) plus an end-to-end application to eICU-CRD v2.0 (164,322 stays, 207 hospitals) under a protocol frozen before the extract was read: alpha=0.10 certifies on all 20 by-site re-splits at 0.890 coverage, alpha=0.05 on none, with candid disclosure that the answered set's mortality (0.046) is roughly half its pool's (0.090).
Strengths: All four reviewers agree the problem is real and precisely framed: record-level selective-risk certificates are the wrong unit under multi-site clustering, and the motivating failure is demonstrated in-harness rather than cited — on identical draws the record-as-unit comparator grants the alpha=0.05 rung the site-unit walk refuses and then violates its aggregate budget at nearly twice delta under high heterogeneity.

The core statistical construction is sound and unusually carefully scoped (verified by one reviewer at the atom-algebra level): bounded per-site atoms tied term-by-term to the estimand, a fixed-sequence walk that spends no extra confidence on multiple looks, and frozen guarantee text with explicit site-population-average, dispersion, parameter-not-count, operative-rung, and concept-exclusion clauses.

The validation and honesty apparatus is well above community standard and praised unanimously: a concept-shift negative control verified capable of failing before it runs, a pre-registered eICU protocol with numbered predictions and failure criteria frozen before the extract was read, falsified predictions reported as falsified, a leak alarm that fired in the unexpected direction analyzed rather than buried, a null attribution result reported as a null, comparator bounds walked on identical atoms, and an influence-cap sensitivity sweep.

The paper is exceptionally frank about its own costs: the answered-set composition disclosure (a constant always-negative rule already meets the alpha=0.10 budget), the measured BBSE box miscoverage, the per-hospital dispersion under a valid certificate, and the subgroup coverage gradient are all volunteered by the authors.

Reproducibility is strong: pinned constants under automated test as a machine-verifiable pre-registration substitute, deterministic seeding with byte-identical certificates, released code including the full eICU extract-to-certificate pipeline, and an aggregate-only release policy for the restricted extract.

The site-count frontier and power frontiers convert abstract validity concerns into concrete capacity planning numbers (alpha=0.05 needs ~300-400 sites; BBSE certification needs ~900-1,200 source sites).
Weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited — a consensus view across all four reviews: the certificate is an assembly of established components (WSR betting martingale, fixed-sequence risk control, cluster-as-unit inference, BBSE with Si-style uncertainty propagation, closed-form linear Shapley attributions), the paper itself identifies prior work sharing the certificate shape over i.i.d. records, and no new statistical theory is claimed; substituting site-level atoms is a natural step, however carefully engineered.

The practical significance of the achievable certificate is questionable — the most heavily weighted consensus concern: at the only issuable rung (alpha=0.10) on eICU, a constant always-negative rule already meets the budget (base error 0.0898); answered-set sensitivity is median 0.126 with derived answered-set FNR 0.80-0.90, so the certificate coexists with calling almost no deaths; the clinically meaningful class-conditional FNR certificate is only issuable at budgets >=0.55 at realistic site counts; and the stricter alpha=0.05 rung requires ~300-400 sites, beyond nearly all real consortia. Honest disclosure does not restore decision-relevant utility.

The label-shift (BBSE) mode — a headline contribution — never issues a certificate in any realistic regime studied (declines all 200 synthetic draws at the registered shift, returns failsafe on all 20 eICU re-splits, and needs ~900-1,200 source sites for positive certification), and three of its four intervals are asymptotic percentile bootstraps with measured joint miscoverage of 0.038 against a nominal <=0.019, so the finite-sample headline claim holds in full only for the exchangeable mode.

The guarantee answers a different question than the clinical motivation poses: it is a site-population average that bounds no individual hospital (one hospital observed at 0.286 answered error under a valid certificate; 7 of 477 per-hospital pools hard-violated), and the two-rung ladder makes the deployed selected claim hold jointly only at 1-2delta = 0.90.

Assumption 1 (i.i.d. site draws) — flagged by the authors themselves as the assumption most at risk — is in tension with the real-data design and left without sensitivity analysis: the 20 re-splits partition one fixed 207-hospital list without replacement rather than drawing from a site population, all sites share the 2014-2015 collection window with unmodeled temporal common shocks, and >=2.9% of patients appear at multiple hospitals.

The real-data evidence base is a single decade-old US cohort whose 20 non-independent re-splits, as the paper concedes, bound only gross violation; pre-registration rests on a dated commit in the authors' own repository rather than a third-party registry.

The practical force of the motivating failure is tempered by the paper's own results: the record-as-unit violation exceeds delta clearly only in the inflated-heterogeneity arm, the real cohort's measured dispersion sits below even the default synthetic arm, and asymptotic cluster-aware bounds (cluster-level t, site bootstrap) grant every rung at essentially nominal fresh-pool exceedance, undercutting the case for the conservative finite-sample test that produces the headline refusal.

The explainability contribution is thin: exact additive attributions of an L2-regularized linear model are elementary, the replicated synthetic attribution study returns a null, and the attributions do not survive non-linear heads.

Presentation is dense and depends heavily on the supplement: many load-bearing quantitative results live in supplementary tables and figures, and the prose leans on long qualification chains, so an expert needs the supplement open to verify most main-text claims.

The measured abstention gradient — coverage falling to 0.82 and answered error rising to 0.075 for patients 75+ — is disclosed as an equity measurement but its deployment consequence (deferred workload and differential selective service concentrated on the oldest and sickest) is not discussed.
Questions: What concrete clinical or audit decision does the certified alpha=0.10 gate support that a constant always-negative rule (error 0.0898 on eICU) does not? Could the certificate be restated on a quantity the trivial rule cannot meet — balanced error, a cost-weighted loss, or a joint error-plus-sensitivity-floor certificate — and would it be issuable at realistic site counts with the same atoms?

The comparator suite shows asymptotic cluster-level t and site-bootstrap bounds granting every rung, including alpha=0.05 at low site counts, at essentially nominal exceedance (0.0508/0.0492). Why should a practitioner accept the finite-sample test's refusal below ~300 sites, and is there a demonstrated regime (cluster count, atom skew, dispersion) where those cluster-aware asymptotic bounds measurably fail while the betting test holds?

Can the BBSE parameter box be made finite-sample (e.g., per-parameter empirical-Bernstein intervals over site atoms) rather than percentile-bootstrap, and at what power cost? As published, what is the implied effective delta of the label-shift certificate given the measured joint miscoverage of 0.038 against nominal <=0.019?

Assumption 1 requires i.i.d. site draws, yet the 20 eICU re-splits partition one fixed 207-hospital list without replacement and all hospitals share the 2014-2015 collection window. Can you quantify, even by simulation in the existing harness, (a) the finite-population perturbation of the betting test's level at this scale and (b) how much common-shock correlation the certificate tolerates before its realized level degrades?

Please state precisely which elements of the certification machinery are new relative to substituting cluster-level atoms into the WSR betting test combined with fixed-sequence risk control, and relative to the closest prior certificate shape over i.i.d. records.

The selected claim holds jointly at only 1-2delta = 0.90 because both rungs are walked. Why not pre-declare a single rung or split delta across rungs, given the paper's own frontier predicts alpha=0.10 is the operative rung at 208 sites? Relatedly, is a subgroup-conditional budget (e.g., a coverage floor for the 75+ band) certifiable on the same atoms, and at what site capacity?
Limitations: All reviewers agree the authors address limitations with unusual thoroughness: the site-average-not-per-site scope, the parameter-not-count distinction, concept shift out of scope, unmodeled temporal common-shock correlation, the symmetric loss and inherited operating point, the single real cohort, cross-hospital patient overlap, and the asymptotic BBSE intervals are all stated in the paper.

Remaining gaps identified across the reviews: (1) the near-vacuity of the certifiable budget relative to trivial baselines at realistic data scales should be framed as a limitation of the framework's clinical value, not only as a disclosure; (2) no quantitative sensitivity analysis exists for violations of the i.i.d.-site assumption the authors themselves flag as most at risk; (3) the human-factors risk that a deployer misreads the 'certified' site-average as a per-hospital or per-patient safety property, giving false reassurance precisely where dispersion is worst; (4) the equity implications of abstention concentrating on the oldest and sickest patients — differential selective service and clinician workload shifted onto the highest-acuity cases — are measured but not discussed as a deployment harm; (5) the practical unverifiability of the assumption tag at a new site from unlabeled data; and (6) data currency, since the demonstrated operating characteristics come from a single 2014-2015 cohort and may not transfer to current case mix and documentation practice.

Strengths: The problem is real and precisely framed: record-level selective-risk certificates are the wrong unit under multi-site clustering, and the paper states its estimand, scope clauses (site-population average, dispersion unbounded, parameter-not-count), and assumption tags with unusual care.

The validation design is well above community standard: a concept-shift negative control verified capable of failing before it runs, a pre-registered protocol on eICU with numbered predictions and failure criteria whose falsifications are reported, comparator bounds walked on identical atoms, an influence-cap sensitivity sweep, and a record-as-unit comparator on the same draws.

Honest disclosure culture: the composition analysis (answered-set mortality 0.046 vs 0.090 in the pool), the admission that a constant always-negative rule meets the alpha=0.10 budget on eICU, and the reporting of the attribution null on the symmetric generator are all commendably frank.

The site-count frontier and power frontiers convert abstract validity concerns into concrete capacity numbers (alpha=0.05 needs ~300-400 sites; BBSE certification needs ~900-1,200 source sites), which is useful planning information.

Reproducibility is strong: pinned constants as a machine-verifiable pre-registration substitute, deterministic byte-identical certificates, released code including the full eICU extract-to-certificate pipeline.
Weaknesses: Methodological novelty is thin for a prestigious ML venue: the certificate is a composition of established components — the WSR betting martingale [7], fixed-sequence risk control [9-11], cluster-as-unit inference in the spirit of [28,29], BBSE [13] with uncertainty propagation following Si et al. [15], and closed-form linear Shapley values [16]. The paper itself identifies Yu & Liu [23] as 'the same certificate shape' over i.i.d. records; substituting site-level atoms is a natural step rather than new theory, and no new statistical results are claimed in the main text.

The practical significance of the achievable certificate is questionable. At the only issuable rung (alpha=0.10) on eICU, a constant always-negative rule already meets the budget (base error 0.0898); answered-set sensitivity is median 0.126 and answered-set FNR 0.80-0.90; and the clinically meaningful class-conditional (FNR) certificate is only issuable at budgets >=0.55 at realistic site counts. The authors disclose this candidly, but disclosure does not restore utility: the deployed guarantee is one a trivial rule satisfies, so what is certified at realistic scale is close to vacuous for the motivating clinical-triage use case.

The central motivating failure is only weakly demonstrated at realistic heterogeneity: the record-as-unit comparator violates its aggregate budget at ~2*delta only in the inflated-heterogeneity arm (su=2.0); at the default arm its violation rate (3.5%) is within delta, and the real cohort's measured dispersion sits below even the default arm. Separately, the paper's own comparator suite shows asymptotic cluster-level t and site-bootstrap bounds granting every rung at essentially nominal fresh-pool exceedance (0.0508 and 0.0492), which undercuts the practical case for the conservative finite-sample test that produces the headline refusal of alpha=0.05 below ~300 sites.

The label-shift mode — the paper's second claimed contribution — never issues a certificate on real data (it fitted and returned failsafe on all re-splits) and requires ~900-1,200 source sites in synthetic experiments; moreover three of its four intervals are asymptotic percentile bootstraps whose measured joint miscoverage is double nominal (0.038 vs <=0.019), so the 'finite-sample' headline holds in full only for the exchangeable mode.

The explainability contribution is slight: exact additive attributions of an L2-regularized logistic model are elementary, the replicated synthetic attribution study returns a null, and the attributions do not survive non-linear heads, scoping the contribution to transparent models.

Real-data evidence is a single 2014-2015 cohort evaluated by 20 non-independent re-splits of one hospital population, which the paper concedes bounds only gross violation; Assumption 1 (i.i.d. site draws) is threatened by unmodeled temporal common shocks and by >=2.9% of patients appearing at multiple hospitals — both acknowledged but unquantified.

Main-text self-containment is weak: many principal results (validity CIs, operating characteristics, frontier tables, composition analyses, subgroup tables) live in Supplementary Tables S2-S9 and Figures S1-S9, and the prose, while precise, is extremely dense.
Questions: What concrete clinical decision does the certified alpha=0.10 gate support that the constant survival-prediction rule (error 0.0898 on eICU) does not? Could the certificate be restated on a quantity the trivial rule cannot meet — balanced error, a cost-weighted loss, or a joint error-plus-sensitivity-floor certificate — and would it be issuable at realistic site counts with the same atoms?

Your comparator suite shows the asymptotic cluster-level t and site-bootstrap bounds granting every rung, including alpha=0.05 at 60 sites, at essentially nominal exceedance (0.0508/0.0492). Why should a practitioner accept the finite-sample test's refusal below ~300 sites rather than the asymptotic cluster bound's grant at nominal risk? Is there a demonstrated regime (cluster count, atom skew) where those cluster-aware asymptotic bounds measurably fail while the betting test holds?

At default heterogeneity the record-as-unit certifier's aggregate violation rate (3.5%) is within delta, and the real cohort's dispersion sits below the default arm. At what measured between-site dispersion does record-level certification actually break its budget, and does eICU plausibly reach it?

Can the BBSE parameter box be made finite-sample (e.g., per-parameter empirical-Bernstein intervals over site atoms) rather than percentile-bootstrap, and at what power cost? As published, the label-shift mode's stated confidence is measurably optimistic (joint miscoverage 0.038 vs nominal <=0.019).

Please state precisely which elements of the certification machinery are new relative to substituting cluster-level atoms in the sense of [28,29] into the WSR betting test [7] combined with fixed-sequence risk control [9,11], and relative to the certificate shape of Yu & Liu [23].

Assumption 1 requires i.i.d. site draws, yet the eICU hospitals share a 2014-2015 collection window and >=2.9% of patients cross hospitals. Can a block-correlated synthetic arm quantify how much common-shock correlation the certificate tolerates before its realized level degrades?
Limitations: The authors address limitations with unusual thoroughness: the site-population-average scope (no per-site bound; one hospital observed at 0.29 answered error), concept shift out of scope, unmodeled temporal common-shock correlation, the single-cohort evidence base, the symmetric loss and inherited operating point, the asymptotic BBSE intervals, and the cross-hospital patient exposure are all stated in the paper.

Remaining concerns: the certified-versus-trivial-baseline vacuity at the issuable rung deserves discussion as a limitation of the framework's clinical value rather than only a disclosure; a deploying hospital may over-trust the 'certified' branding as a per-site safety property despite the dispersion clause, a plausible negative societal impact in triage settings; and the eICU cohort is a decade old, so the demonstrated operating characteristics may not transfer to current case mix and documentation practice.

Each calibration site is compressed into a bounded atom and a Waudby-Smith-Ramdas betting martingale is walked over a fixed-sequence threshold grid at two budget rungs (alpha in {0.05, 0.10}). The gate ships two assumption modes: an exchangeable baseline, and a BBSE label-shift mode that propagates the estimation uncertainty of four corrected parameters into the guarantee via a Bonferroni box of cluster-robust intervals. A linear head supplies exact additive attributions for both answers and abstentions. Evaluation covers nine synthetic experiment families on a 208-site generator with oracle access (validity, label-shift stress, a verified-falsifiable concept-shift negative control, site-count frontier, attribution replication, coverage/composition, a record-as-unit comparator, alternative-bound and stress suites, and power frontiers), plus an end-to-end application to eICU-CRD v2.0 (164,322 stays, 207 hospitals) under a protocol frozen before the extract was read: alpha=0.10 certifies on all 20 by-site re-splits at 0.890 coverage, alpha=0.05 on none, and the answered set's mortality (0.046) is roughly half its pool's (0.090), a composition cost the paper discloses.
Strengths: The core diagnosis is correct and demonstrated rather than asserted: on identical draws the record-as-unit certifier grants the alpha=0.05 rung the site-unit walk refuses and then violates its aggregate budget at nearly twice delta under high heterogeneity (Section 4.8), which turns the motivating citation into an in-harness result.

The statistical machinery is carefully assembled and correctly scoped: bounded per-site atoms tied term-by-term to the estimand, a fixed-sequence walk that spends no extra confidence on multiple looks, Ville's inequality for the finite-sample level, and a frozen guarantee text whose clauses (site-population average, dispersion unbounded, parameter-not-count, concept shift out of scope) are unusually precise about what is and is not promised.

The validation design can fail and sometimes does: a concept-shift negative control verified capable of raising answered error before it is run, a comparator suite of four alternative bounds on identical atoms showing the asymptotic defaults certify invalidly while the betting test dominates the valid ones, an aleatoric stress arm showing decline-before-violate behavior, and an influence-cap sweep.

The eICU study is executed with pre-registration discipline rare in ML: a protocol, feature allowlist, leak denylist, seven predictions and five failure criteria committed before the extract was read; falsified predictions reported as falsified; a leak alarm that fired in the unexpected direction reported honestly; a single post-hoc amendment labeled as such.

The paper is exceptionally honest about its own costs: the answered-set composition disclosure (a constant always-negative rule already meets the alpha=0.10 budget), the measured BBSE box miscoverage (0.038 vs nominal 0.019), the per-hospital dispersion (a certified run containing a hospital at 0.286 answered error), and the subgroup coverage gradient into the oldest and sickest are all volunteered.
Reproducibility is strong: pinned constants under automated test, deterministic seeding, byte-identical certificates, released code, and an aggregate-only release policy for the restricted extract.
Weaknesses: Limited practical significance of what is actually certifiable: at realistic scale the only certificate the method issues is alpha=0.10 on a cohort whose base error rate is 0.0898, a budget the paper concedes a constant predict-survival rule already meets; the answered set's median sensitivity at the inherited threshold is 0.126 and the derived answered-set FNR is 0.80-0.90. The guarantee is real, but what it guarantees on this cohort is close to what a trivial rule achieves, and the class-conditional (FNR) budget experiment shows no clinically meaningful FNR budget (below ~0.55) is issuable at realistic site counts.

The two genuinely novel modes deliver no positive result at realistic capacity: the BBSE label-shift mode declines all 200 synthetic draws at the registered shift and certifies nothing on eICU (its demonstrated value is the refusal itself), with positive certification measured to require roughly 900-1,200 source sites; and its printed confidence is admittedly not finite-sample (three of four intervals are asymptotic percentile bootstraps with measured joint miscoverage 0.038 against nominal <=0.019), so the headline 'finite-sample' claim holds in full only for the exchangeable mode.

Methodological novelty is a combination of existing components (WSR betting, fixed-sequence testing, cluster-as-unit atoms, BBSE, Bonferroni parameter boxes, closed-form linear attributions); the paper is well positioned against near-neighbors ([23], [28-29], [15], [33]) but contributes no new theory, and the attribution contribution is essentially standard for a linear model.

The real-data validity evidence is weak relative to the claim: 20 by-site re-splits partition one fixed 207-hospital list rather than drawing fresh sites from a population, which does not match Assumption 1's i.i.d. site draw (the authors note a without-replacement variant as future work), and the paper itself concedes twenty re-splits cannot resolve a 0.05 violation rate; the evidence base is a single cohort from 2014-2015.

The certified estimand is a site-population average that bounds no individual hospital: on the certified real-data runs one hospital sits at 0.286 answered error and 7 of 477 per-hospital pools are hard-violated. The paper discloses this clearly, but it means the certificate answers a question (consortium-average risk) that is arguably not the one a deploying hospital or its auditor asks.

The selected claim on the two-rung ladder holds jointly only at 1-2*delta = 0.90, and pre-registration credibility rests on a dated commit in the authors' own repository, both acknowledged but weakening the headline confidence.

Presentation is dense: most quantitative evidence lives in supplementary figures and tables (S1-S9), the prose leans on long qualification chains, and an expert would need the supplement open to verify most Section 4 claims from the main text.
Questions: Clinical utility: given answered-set sensitivity ~0.126 and answered-set FNR 0.80-0.90 on eICU, what clinical decision would the certified alpha=0.10 gate support that a constant predict-survival rule (error 0.0898) would not? Can you exhibit any head/operating-point on this cohort where certification coexists with clinically useful sensitivity, or is that impossible at 74 calibration clusters?

Assumption 1 vs the re-split design: the 20 by-site re-splits sample calibration and target sites without replacement from a fixed 207-hospital list, not i.i.d. from a superpopulation. Can you quantify (even by simulation) how much the finite-population effect perturbs the betting test's level at this scale, and why is the without-replacement variant deferred rather than reported?

BBSE box coverage: the design-time probe measured joint miscoverage 0.038 against nominal <=0.019. What is the implied effective delta of the label-shift certificate, and could the percentile bootstraps be replaced by finite-sample per-parameter bounds (e.g., empirical-Bernstein over clusters) so the mode's confidence statement matches the paper's finite-sample framing?

The selected claim holds at 1-2*delta = 0.90 because both rungs are walked. Why not pre-declare a single rung (or split delta across rungs) to preserve 0.95, given that Section 3.5 already predicts alpha=0.10 is the operative rung at 208 sites?

How should a new consortium choose the influence cap M a priori? The sweep shows a plateau for M<=100 on this size distribution, but the choice is described as substantive ('whose errors count'); is there a principled rule beyond the pinned default?

Subgroups: coverage falls to 0.82 and answered error rises to 0.075 for patients 75+, with the same gradient across admission acuity. Is a subgroup-conditional budget certifiable on the same atoms, and at what site capacity?
Limitations: The authors' own limitations section is unusually thorough: site-average-only guarantee, concept shift out of scope, unmodeled temporal common-shock correlation (the assumption most at risk), symmetric loss with an inherited operating point, single real cohort, cross-hospital patient overlap, and asymptotic BBSE intervals are all stated.

Two points deserve more weight than they receive: (1) the mismatch between Assumption 1's i.i.d. site draw and the finite-population re-split design used for all real-data evidence; (2) the societal implication of the measured abstention gradient - the gate defers most on the oldest and sickest patients, so deployment would concentrate clinician workload, and any misreading of the site-average certificate as a per-hospital or per-patient promise could give false reassurance precisely where dispersion is worst. The paper measures the gradient but does not discuss its downstream care implications.
The value of the certificate relative to trivial baselines at achievable budgets should be framed as a limitation of the approach at current data scales, not only as a disclosure.

If not, what concrete deployment decision does the certificate improve over simply reporting the trivial always-negative rule's error with a cluster-robust interval?

Given median answered-set sensitivity 0.126 and answered FNR 0.80-0.90 on eICU, what is the intended clinical role of an answered case? Should the class-conditional FNR budget of Section 4.13 have been the primary certificate, and if so, is the honest conclusion that no clinically meaningful budget is certifiable at this scale?

The BBSE box's measured joint miscoverage is 0.038 against a nominal <=0.019, so the label-shift mode's stated 1-delta is not achieved. Why is this mode still presented as carrying its uncertainty 'inside the guarantee', and is a finite-sample cluster-valid interval construction feasible to replace the percentile bootstraps?

The abstract reports the synthetic validity result 'inside delta = 0.05', while the operative-rung selection makes the deployed claim jointly 1-2delta = 0.90. Please state the operative confidence explicitly wherever the certificate is headlined.

How do violations of Assumption 1 via shared temporal shocks (sites correlated through a common collection window) quantitatively affect the certificate? A simulation arm injecting common-shock correlation seems within easy reach of the existing harness.

On eICU the 20 re-splits repartition one fixed set of 207 hospitals. In what sense does this validate a guarantee whose probability is taken over draws from a site population, and what would change in the claims if the eICU hospital list were treated as the finite population itself?
Limitations: The limitations section is unusually thorough and candid: no per-site bound, concept shift out of scope, temporal common-shock correlation unmodeled, symmetric loss with an inherited operating point, one real cohort, cross-hospital patient overlap, and the BBSE bootstrap shortfall are all stated by the authors.
Missing: any quantitative sensitivity analysis for violations of the i.i.d.-site assumption (the assumption the authors themselves flag as most at risk).

Missing: discussion of automation-bias risk when a gate labeled 'certified' answers 89% of cases while calling almost no deaths - a clinician may over-trust answered 'survive' calls; the composition disclosures mitigate but do not analyze this human-factors risk.
The data currency limitation (a single 2014-2015 US cohort) deserves explicit statement given the deployment framing.

final_reviews_full.Summary: The paper presents CertGate, a selective-prediction gate for multi-site clinical risk models that certifies, with finite-sample confidence 1-delta, that the influence-weighted error rate among answered cases stays at or below a budget alpha, treating the hospital (site) rather than the record as the unit of statistical independence. Each calibration site is compressed into one bounded atom and a Waudby-Smith-Ramdas betting martingale tests the site-level mean against the budget, with an operating threshold chosen by a fixed-sequence walk that spends no extra confidence. The gate ships two assumption modes named in the guarantee text: an exchangeable baseline, and a label-shift (BBSE) mode that propagates the estimation uncertainty of all four corrected parameters into the budget via a Bonferroni box of cluster-robust intervals. A linear head gives every answer and abstention exact additive attributions. Evaluation covers nine synthetic experiment families with oracle access (validity grid, label-shift stress, verified-falsifiable concept-shift negative control, site-count frontier, attribution study, coverage/composition, record-as-unit comparator, alternative-certifier and stress suite, power frontiers) plus an end-to-end study on eICU-CRD v2.0 (164,322 stays, 207 hospitals) under a protocol frozen before the extract was read: alpha=0.10 certifies on all 20 by-site re-splits at 0.890 coverage; alpha=0.05 on none; the record-as-unit comparator grants the stricter rung and then violates its aggregate budget at nearly twice delta under heterogeneity.
Strengths: The problem is real and well motivated: record-level selective-risk certificates are shown (not just cited) to be overconfident under grouped deployment - the record-as-unit comparator on identical draws certifies the rung the site-unit walk refuses and then violates its aggregate budget at ~2x delta under high heterogeneity, a genuinely useful demonstration for the risk-control community.

The core construction is technically sound. I verified the atom algebra: Z_c = alpha + g_c a_c (e_c - alpha)/M is bounded in [0,1] with E[Z] <= alpha iff R_M <= alpha; the fixed-sequence walk validly spends no extra confidence on multiple thresholds; the guarantee text is frozen with explicit estimand, dispersion, parameter-not-count, operative-rung, and concept-exclusion clauses.

The validation design is unusually honest and complete: negative controls verified capable of failing before being run, a null attribution result reported as a null, falsified pre-registered predictions reported, sensitivity sweeps of the one influential frozen constant, four alternative cluster-aware bounds confirming the site-count frontier on identical atoms, and an aleatoric stress arm showing the certifier declines before it violates.

The real-data study follows a protocol frozen before the extract was read, with an attrition ledger recording deaths at each step, pre-declared leak screens (one of which fired in the informative inverted direction and is analyzed rather than buried), and candid disclosures - including that a constant always-negative rule already meets the alpha=0.10 budget at this prevalence and that part of the budget is met by abstaining where deaths concentrate.

Reproducibility appears strong: deterministic seeding, byte-identical certificates on identical inputs, pinned constants enforced by an automated test, released code with a single-command synthetic grid.
Weaknesses: Clinical utility of the achievable guarantee is questionable. At 8.9% prevalence the operative alpha=0.10 budget is met by a trivial always-negative rule (erring at 0.0898, admitted in Section 4.10); answered-set sensitivity has median 0.126 and the derived answered-set FNR is 0.80-0.90, so the certificate coexists with calling almost no deaths. The class-conditional FNR budget is only issuable at >=0.55 at realistic site counts. The paper prices this honestly, but honesty does not create decision-relevant value at the certifiable rung.

The label-shift contribution underdelivers on its own framing: three of the four BBSE intervals are asymptotic percentile bootstraps with a measured joint miscoverage of 0.038 against a nominal <=0.019, so the shipped mode does not hold its stated finite-sample level; and on the real cohort the mode fitted but certified nothing - positive certification is demonstrated only at 900-1,200 synthetic source sites. Contribution 2 is, at realistic scale, a demonstrated refusal.

The guarantee is a site-population average with individual hospitals explicitly unbounded - the real cohort exhibits a hospital at 0.2857 answered error under a valid certificate (7 of 477 pools hard-violated). For the clinician or auditor at one hospital, the certificate's operational meaning is limited; a per-site quantile bound is deferred to future work.

Assumption 1 (i.i.d. site draws) is in tension with the real-data design: the 20 re-splits partition one fixed 207-hospital list (without-replacement, acknowledged as future work), all sites share the 2014-2015 collection window, and temporal common-shock correlation is unmodeled - the assumption most at risk is unquantified exactly where the headline result lives.

Methodological novelty is a combination of off-the-shelf parts (WSR betting, fixed-sequence testing, cluster-as-unit atoms, BBSE, Si-style uncertainty propagation, closed-form linear Shapley); the combination is engineered carefully but each piece is standard, and the explainability contribution in particular is thin - exact attributions for a linear model are elementary and the synthetic attribution study returns a null.

Real-data evidence is one cohort, and 20 re-splits cannot resolve the delta=0.05 rate (the paper concedes it bounds gross violation only); the pre-registration is a self-controlled repository commit rather than a third-party registry.

Abstention concentrates on the oldest and sickest (coverage 0.96 to 0.82 and answered error 0.019 to 0.075 into the 75+ band): disclosed as a measured equity property, but the deployment consequence - differential selective service and deferred workload precisely for the most vulnerable subgroup - deserves more than measurement.

The paper is dense, stylistically idiosyncratic, and leans heavily on supplementary tables (S2-S9) for load-bearing results; the two-rung ladder yields a joint selected-claim confidence of only 1-2delta = 0.90.
Questions: Given that a constant always-negative rule meets the alpha=0.10 budget at this prevalence and answered-set sensitivity is ~0.13, can you articulate a concrete deployment decision that the certified quantity changes? What would an auditor do differently with this certificate versus without it?

The BBSE box's measured joint miscoverage (0.038 vs nominal <=0.019) means the shipped label-shift mode exceeds its stated error share by roughly 2x. Why ship the asymptotic bootstrap rather than repair with a finite-sample per-parameter bound (e.g., empirical-Bernstein or DKW-based), even at some power cost, given the paper's finite-sample framing?

How much does the finite-population, without-replacement structure of the 20 eICU re-splits (partitioning a fixed 207-hospital list) quantitatively distort the nominal level of the betting test relative to Assumption 1's i.i.d. draw? Even a simulation under the synthetic generator with without-replacement site sampling would help.
Why only two rungs {0.05, 0.10}? A finer alpha ladder with the same fixed-sequence discipline (or alpha-spending) could yield a more informative operative budget than a binary certify/refuse at 0.10.
Coverage and answered error degrade monotonically into the 75+ age band. Have you considered a per-subgroup coverage floor or a stratified certificate, and what would it cost in calibration clusters?

Is there any diagnostic a deployer can run on unlabeled target data to gain evidence that the exchangeable tag (rather than neither tag) applies, short of the concept-shift impossibility - e.g., feature-distribution screens that would at least flag gross covariate shift?
Limitations: The authors are unusually forthcoming: the site-average-not-per-site scope, the parameter-not-count distinction, the concept-shift exclusion, the BBSE bootstrap miscoverage, the trivial-baseline comparison, the composition cost (answered mortality 0.046 vs 0.090 in pool), the single-cohort limit, the unmodeled temporal correlation, and the cross-hospital patient exposure are all stated in the paper.

Remaining under-addressed items: the equity implications of abstention concentrating on the oldest and sickest patients (differential selective service and clinician workload shifted onto the highest-acuity cases) are measured but not discussed as a deployment harm; and the practical unverifiability of the tagged assumption at a new site (a deployer cannot confirm from unlabeled data which tag, if any, applies) deserves explicit treatment as a limitation of the certificate's real-world interpretability.
